claims.claim: Scholarship documents that women characters in early and classical Hollywood cinema were frequently cast within a narrow binary — chaste and virtuous or sexualized and dangerous — a pattern film critics have traced from the silent era through later decades, including its variations in film noir and 1950s domestic comedies.

In 'Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema' (1975), film theorist Laura Mulvey argued that classical narrative cinema organizes looking along gendered lines, positioning women as images to be looked at and men as bearers of the look.
Mulvey's essay identifies three looks in narrative cinema: the look of the camera, the look of the spectator, and the look of the characters within the film.

The male gaze is an influential theory rather than a settled fact; critics have questioned its assumption of a unified spectator, scholars such as bell hooks developed alternative accounts (the 'oppositional gaze'), and Mulvey herself revisited female spectatorship in later work.

Feminist film scholarship developed accounts of the female gaze and female spectatorship (including work by Mary Ann Doane and Lorraine Gamman), and queer film scholarship developed queer readings of mainstream texts (including Alexander Doty's 1993 book Making Things Perfectly Queer and Karen Hollinger's work on the lesbian gaze).

Women remain a minority in key behind-the-camera roles on the top-grossing U.S. films: in 2025 women comprised 13% of directors and 7% of cinematographers on the top 250 films, and 23% of directors, writers, producers, executive producers, editors, and cinematographers combined; 75% of the top 250 films employed 10 or more men in pivotal behind-the-scenes roles while only 7% employed 10 or more women.

A separate university study found that 12.1% of the directors of the 100 top-grossing U.S. films of 2023 were women, a share judged 'not meaningfully different' from 2022, and that across 2007-2023 the ratio of individual men to women directors was about 9.8 to 1.

On-screen measures of the top-grossing U.S. films of 2025: 29% had female protagonists (down from 42% in 2024), 38% of speaking roles were female, 82% of films featured more male than female speaking characters, and women aged 60 and older made up 2% of major female characters (versus 8% of major male characters); the report itself cautions that the protagonist figure is volatile because it rests on the top 100 films, while speaking-role figures are more stable.

The Bechdel test originated in Alison Bechdel's 1985 comic strip Dykes to Watch Out For (with the idea credited to Liz Wallace and Virginia Woolf), became widely used in the 2000s as shorthand for whether women are present in a work, and functions as a minimal threshold: passing or failing does not indicate the overall quality or depth of a work's representation.
The concept of gendered looking predates Mulvey: art critic John Berger argued in Ways of Seeing (1972) that Western art tradition positions men as lookers and women as being looked at.

Describing patterns in media is a claim about texts and industries, not about inherent traits of any group; scholarship notes, for example, that having a woman director does not by itself guarantee any particular kind of film, since filmmakers work within shared industrial conventions.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does the male gaze describe every viewer's experience?
positions: Mulvey's 1975 essay argues that the structure of classical narrative cinema positions the spectator to look along with the male protagonist at the woman as image

Critics and later scholars argued the theory assumes a unified spectator and underplays female spectatorship, racial difference, and queer viewing positions (e.g., hooks' oppositional gaze; Doane and Gamman on the female spectator; Hollinger on the lesbian gaze)
Mulvey herself revisited female spectatorship in later work
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the male gaze as an attributed theory with documented critiques and later scholarly developments, not as an empirical law about all viewers.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the year-to-year female-protagonist percentage a reliable indicator of progress?
positions: 29% of the top 100 grossing films of 2025 had female protagonists, down sharply from 42% in 2024
The SDSU report itself cautions that this top-100-based figure fluctuates dramatically with small changes, while speaking-role and major-character percentages are more stable
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports the numbers together with the report's own methodological caution.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does the Bechdel test measure quality of representation?
positions: The test is widely used as shorthand for whether women are present and talking in a film
Its own documentation and critics note that passing is a minimal threshold about presence that says little about depth, quality, or equality of representation
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the test as a heuristic with explicit limits and no claim to measure quality.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Are behind-the-camera gender disparities narrowing or stalled?
positions: USC Annenberg's report across 2007-2023 concludes that progress for women directors has stalled

SDSU's Celluloid Ceiling shows some roles rising slowly over 25 years (directors 9% in 1998 to 13% in 2025) while others are flat (editors 20% in both years), and its Boxed In report documents larger recent gains in streaming television
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports both trends with their sources and avoids a single narrative of progress or stagnation.

sourceRecords.title: Women in Cinema
sourceRecords.provider: University of Arkansas Libraries Pressbooks / Russell Leigh Sharman
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-21. Chapter of the open textbook Moving Pictures (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). Supports: historical patterns of women's roles in Hollywood (the virgin-temptress binary as applied by film critics), a summary of Laura Mulvey's 1975 essay and the male gaze, the origin of the Bechdel test in Alison Bechdel's 1985 comic strip, the historical rarity of women behind the camera (Alice Guy-Blaché, Lois Weber, Ida Lupino), and the caution that a woman director does not by itself determine a film's content. Lesson prose is original synthesis; no film dialogue, stills, or source wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Visual Pleasure and Narrative Cinema (1975)
sourceRecords.provider: Laura Mulvey; copy hosted by Arizona State University course materials
sourceRecords.notes: Primary scholarly essay, originally published in the journal Screen 16.3 (Autumn 1975). Read as the ASU-hosted scanned copy (verified 7-page PDF, version 1.3). Because the scan has no text layer, the essay's content claims used in this lesson were cross-checked against two independent scholarly summaries (the Moving Pictures 'Women in Cinema' chapter and Wikipedia's 'Male gaze' article). Supports the essay's existence, 1975 publication, and its core argument that classical narrative cinema structures looking along gendered lines (woman as image, man as bearer of the look; scopophilia, voyeurism, and narcissistic identification). Facts synthesized in original wording.
